title.title: Diophantine sets with exactly one witness
title.subtitle: Claim: every computably enumerable set has a polynomial representation with exactly one witness per member

beats.text: Every computably enumerable set is where a polynomial has an integer witness $w$
Matiyasevich asked in 1974 for exactly one witness per member
The claim: yes, with points $nP$ on a rank-one elliptic curve in place of Pell equations

sources.ref: article, Hilbert's tenth problem over Q (family 004)
sources.quote: Matiyasevich showed in 1970 that no algorithm decides whether an integer polynomial has an integer root.
Matiyasevich (1974) proved single-fold exponential Diophantine representations and posed the polynomial single-fold (and finite-fold) problem
an integer polynomial P(a, w) such that for a in S there is exactly one witness tuple w in N^m with P(a, w) = 0 and for a not in S there is none
Diophantine solvability over N stays undecidable under the promise of at most one solution
Uses a rank-one elliptic curve and Neron-Tate height to get a single-fold growth relation replacing Pell-equation exponentiation.
main theorem formalized (SingleFold.main); the promise-undecidability consequence not separately formalized.
only `propext`, `Quot.sound` and `Classical.choice` for every family here

plain: Every list a computer can generate is the set of inputs where one equation has exactly one solution

steps: Known: exactly one witness works if exponentials are allowed
Encode exponentials with points $nP$ on an elliptic curve
Each $n$ has one point, so the witness stays unique

voice.text: Every computable list is where a polynomial has a solution. Matiyasevich asked for exactly one.
Points on an elliptic curve encode exponentials, exactly one point per number.
Claimed: exactly one witness, for every list.
